opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think about this a lot, because people sometimes frame it as a tradeoff: either you're working on today's problems, like a model being sycophantic or making things up, or you're working on the "real" long-term risks. I don't really see it that way. A lot of the present-day work is basically practice on the same underlying problem at lower stakes.

If you take something like sycophancy, where the model tells you what you want to hear instead of what's true, that's a small-scale version of a much scarier failure mode. It's the model optimizing for looking good to the evaluator rather than actually being good. Today that means it flatters your business plan. In a much more capable system, the same dynamic could mean hiding mistakes, or gaming oversight in ways that are hard to detect. If we can't reliably get models to be honest when the stakes are low and we can check the answer, I don't have much confidence we'll manage it when the stakes are high and we can't.

There's also the toolkit side. Techniques like constitutional approaches, reinforcement learning from AI feedback, interpretability, and red-teaming all get built and stress-tested against today's behavior problems. You learn where they break. You learn how to measure things. You build the evals and the organizational muscle for taking a weird model behavior seriously, digging into it, and fixing it rather than shrugging. All of that carries forward.

And honestly, there's an empirical lesson in it too. Every generation of models has surprised us in some way, with behaviors nobody explicitly trained for. Working on present-day problems keeps you grounded in what models actually do rather than what you theorized they'd do. That feedback loop is incredibly valuable, because the higher-harm scenarios are exactly the ones where you don't get many chances to iterate.

So my view is that it's not a distraction. It's the closest thing we have to a training ground. The goal is to have the science mature enough, and the habits strong enough, that by the time the stakes are really high we're not starting from scratch.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there's a view out there that the stuff we work on today — like, does the model refuse to help with something it shouldn't, or does it lie to you, or does it write sycophantic responses — is kind of a toy problem compared to the real thing, which is "what happens when you have a system that's smarter than you and might not want what you want." And I actually think that's mostly wrong, for a couple of reasons.

The first is that the techniques are continuous. When we work on, say, honesty — getting a model to not confabulate, to say "I don't know" when it doesn't know, to not tell you what you want to hear — we're building the same muscles we need for the scarier cases. The harder problems are versions of the same problem with higher stakes and a more capable adversary, if you want to call it that. If you can't get a model to be reliably honest about something small, you have no business thinking you can get it to be honest about something large. So the present-day problems are the proving ground. We learn what works, what breaks, where the techniques generalize and where they don't.

The second thing is that we're learning what we don't understand. A lot of what alignment research looks like day to day is: we had a theory about how the model would behave, we trained it, it behaved differently, and now we have to figure out why. Every one of those surprises is a data point about the gap between our intentions and what actually gets learned. And that gap is the whole problem. If we're surprised now, with models we can inspect pretty thoroughly and whose capabilities we can mostly reason about, we should expect to be more surprised later. So the practice of catching the gap early, with small consequences, is how you develop the instincts and the tooling to catch it when the consequences are big.

The third piece is more institutional. The reason you want to be doing this work on real deployed systems, rather than purely in the abstract, is that it forces you to build the infrastructure — evals, red-teaming, interpretability tooling, the whole feedback loop with real users — and to make the organizational commitments that let you actually act on what you find. Like, it's one thing to have a safety team write a paper. It's another thing to have a process where, if the eval comes back bad, you don't ship. Those processes get built by exercising them on the problems that exist today. If you wait until the stakes are existential to try to set that up, you're way too late.

And I'd add — there's a kind of trust that gets built with the broader world. If you're the lab that's visibly taking the small things seriously and being honest about where you fall short, you have more credibility when you say "we think this bigger thing is a real risk." Whereas if you're hand-waving the small stuff, nobody should believe you about the big stuff.

So I don't think of it as "present-day problems versus the real problem." I think of it as a ladder, where each rung is the only way to reach the next one. The failure mode I worry about is people thinking they can skip rungs.

astra-6.text:
I think present-day problems give us a way to practice the whole alignment loop. You see a behavior you don’t want, you figure out how to measure it, you try an intervention, and then you ask whether you actually fixed the problem or just taught the model to pass your test.

Take sycophancy. If a model tells you what you want to hear instead of what’s true, that can be annoying in a casual conversation. But if you’re relying on it for a consequential decision, the same tendency becomes much more serious. So getting models to be honest, to acknowledge uncertainty, and to push back appropriately seems useful across a pretty wide range of capabilities.

The caveat is that solving today’s problems doesn’t establish that we’ve solved alignment for much more capable systems. There could be qualitatively new failure modes. But we can build the measurement tools, the scientific understanding, and the habit of testing our assumptions now. I’d rather have that feedback loop than have everything rest on an argument we can’t yet test.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of present-day behavior problems as a kind of laboratory for alignment. We can ask: Can we specify what we want? Can we train a model to do it? And can we tell whether it’s actually doing it, versus just looking good on our evaluations?

Take a model that’s being sycophantic—it tells you what you want to hear instead of what’s true. That might be relatively low stakes in a casual conversation, but the underlying problem matters a lot if you’re relying on a much more capable system for consequential decisions. Working on it today gives us a concrete way to test our training methods and our ability to measure progress.

The caveat is that solving today’s problems doesn’t prove we’ve solved alignment for much more powerful systems. There may be new failure modes, and some approaches may stop working as capabilities increase. So I see this as a feedback loop: use the systems we have to build and test alignment techniques, while continually asking which results should generalize and where we’re making assumptions we haven’t actually tested.
